# Imports 
```{r}
library(e1071)
```

# Scale the numerical data. 
```{r}
# Scaling numerical data refers to transforming numerical features to a common scale, which stops features from dominating others

# ! This was much easier to easier to do using the scale function
data <- read.csv("week4_data.csv")
head(data) # print first few lines
str(data) # print structure
# ! Note: this data has NA! So we're going to drop those values

# get only numeric data
numeric_data <- data[sapply(data, is.numeric)]
scaled_data <- scale(numeric_data)
# It transforms each numerical variable (column) to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
head(scaled_data)
```

# Fix any skew as best you can.
```{r}
#! Note: I might have done this part wrong because I used data instead of the scaled data.

# This is fairly open ended, but from our book we determine that skewness pushes a normal distribution to the left or the right. We can clean up skewness by dropping outliers or using a log transformation.


# As a reminder, skew looks like this:
# Close to 0 - Perfect!
# Above 0 - Right skewed
# Below 0 - Left skewed


# Another way to view skew is to say "Which way does the tail go? Tail left = left skewed, tail right = right skewed

# First, we can check the overall skewness of the data
skewness_cols <- c("critic_score", "total_sales", "na_sales", "jp_sales", "pal_sales", "other_sales")
skewed_values <- sapply(data[skewness_cols], skewness, na.rm = TRUE)
skewed_values

# This was not what I expected...our skewness shows critics skewed left skewed, but the rest are heavily right skewed. To double check, we're going to visualize it with a histogram
hist(data$critic_score, breaks = 30, main = "Critic Score", col = "lightblue") # critic was -.9 and showed a weak tail on the left, about what we expected
hist(data$total_sales, breaks = 30, main = "Total Sales", col = "lightblue") # sales was massively skewed in comparison at 8.0, so the very small right tail was expected

right_skewed_cols <- c("total_sales", "na_sales", "jp_sales", "pal_sales", "other_sales")
left_skewed_cols <- c("critic_score")

# left skew fixes
data$critic_score_log <- data$critic_score^2
hist(data$critic_score_log, breaks = 30, main = "Total Scores", col = "lightblue") # this shows an improvement in skewness and the shape is slightly better

skewed_critic_score <- skewness(data$critic_score_log, na.rm = TRUE)
skewed_critic_score # this went from -.9 to -.3, so we improved the skewness, but the graph shows a much larger improvement

# right skew fixes
# There are a few here, so we'll start with total sales first
data$total_sales_log <- log(data$total_sales + 1)
hist(data$total_sales_log, breaks = 30, main = "Total Sales", col = "lightblue") # this improved some skewness but the overall shape is still right skewed

# Lets try similar fixes to the other right skews
data$na_sales_log <- log(data$na_sales + 1)
hist(data$na_sales_log, breaks = 30, main = "na_sales", col = "lightblue") # This was the same as the total sales in terms of distribution.

data$jp_sales_log <- log(data$jp_sales + 1)
hist(data$jp_sales_log, breaks = 30, main = "jp_sales", col = "lightblue") # This was the same as the total sales in terms of distribution.

# Do the same for pal_sales and other_sales
data$pal_sales_log <- log(data$pal_sales + 1)
hist(data$pal_sales_log, breaks = 30, main = "pal_sales", col = "lightblue")

data$other_sales_log <- log(data$other_sales + 1)
hist(data$other_sales_log, breaks = 30, main = "other_sales", col = "lightblue")

# This other_sales_log is still HEAVILY skewed, but it has been improved
```


# Normalize any columns not normalized using any of the available techniques (don’t use the same technique twice).
```{r}
# There are several ways to standardize:
#   - Z-score normalization - subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation
#   - Min-max normalization - subtract the min and divide by the range
#   - Decimal scaling - divide by 10^j, where j is the number of digits in the max value
#   - Robust normalization - subtract the median and divide by the interquartile range

# We have several cols to use for scaling. Currently, none of them are normalized to 0-1, so let's use each of the normalization techniques on a different column

# Z-score normalization
data$z_score_normalized <- (data$critic_score - mean(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)

# Min-max normalization
data$min_max_normalized <- (data$critic_score - min(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE) - min(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE))

# Decimal scaling
j <- ceiling(log10(max(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)))
data$decimal_scaled <- data$critic_score / (10^j)

# Robust normalization
data$robust_normalized <- (data$critic_score - median(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)) / IQR(data$critic_score, na.rm = TRUE)

head(data)
```

# Using data simulation, fill in the missing values for the release_date variable (not the others).
```{r}
# There are several ways to do data simulation. I chose to use the mean of the release_date column, which ended up being november 14, 2006

# First, got get all dates where the date is na. I also checked for empty because that's what I kept seeing
data_missing <- data[data$release_date == "", ]
head(data_missing) # print to make sure we found them

# filter to only use data where dates have a value
data_with_dates <- data$release_date[data$release_date != ""]

# get the mean date. We could've made another dataframe, but i just filtered the original data WITHOUT
mean_date <- mean(as.Date(data_with_dates, origin = "1970-01-01"), na.rm = TRUE)

data_missing$release_date <- mean_date
head(data_missing)
```
